Whoring
HOR-ing
v. (participle)
From Old English hore. The Authorized Version’s idiom is to go a whoring after, rendering a Hebrew verb for harlotry used figuratively of idolatry. The translators chose the coarse word deliberately, because God had chosen the coarse figure deliberately.

Biblical Definition

Whoring is the Authorized Version’s rendering of God’s own metaphor for idolatry, and He uses it without apology. The covenant at Sinai is a marriage, and the worship of another god is therefore adultery, not a difference of religious opinion. The warning is issued before Israel enters the land: lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods… And thou take of their daughters unto thy sons, and their daughters go a whoring after their gods, and make thy sons go a whoring after their gods (Exodus 34:15-16). The book of Judges records the outcome in a single sentence: they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods (Judges 2:17). Even a good man’s well-meant relic can become the object — Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house (Judges 8:27). And the psalm turns the figure inward, past foreign gods altogether: they were defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions (Psalm 106:39). Idolatry does not require a foreign shrine. A man’s own inventions will serve.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WHOREDOM in its scriptural sense as idolatry, the desertion of the worship of the true God for the worship of idols — noting the figurative use directly. The English coarseness is the point: God is describing a betrayal of the most intimate covenant.

expand to see more

WHORING, ppr. — In Scripture, following after idols; committing spiritual fornication.

WHOREDOM, n. — In Scripture, idolatry; the desertion of the worship of the true God, for the worship of idols.

Webster records the figurative sense as a proper scriptural definition, not as a curiosity — the usage was familiar to every reader of the Authorized Version.

The idiom to go a whoring after preserves an old English construction with the prefixed particle, as in a-hunting and a-fishing.

Hosea is the sustained working out of the figure, with the prophet’s own marriage as the living parable.

Key Scripture

Exodus 34:15 — "Lest thou make a covenant with the inhabitants of the land, and they go a whoring after their gods, and do sacrifice unto their gods, and one call thee, and thou eat of his sacrifice;"

Judges 2:17 — "And yet they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods, and bowed themselves unto them: they turned quickly out of the way which their fathers walked in, obeying the commandments of the LORD; but they did not so."

Judges 8:27 — "And Gideon made an ephod thereof, and put it in his city, even in Ophrah: and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house."

Psalm 106:39 — "Thus were they defiled with their own works, and went a whoring with their own inventions."

1 Chronicles 5:25 — "And they transgressed against the God of their fathers, and went a whoring after the gods of the people of the land, whom God destroyed before them."

Modern Corruption

The metaphor itself is now the offence. Modern readers object to God’s language as demeaning, and modern translations often soften it — which removes precisely the covenantal shock the figure was given to produce.

expand to see more

Feminist and progressive readings of Hosea and Ezekiel 16 and 23 charge the prophets with degrading imagery, and some evangelical commentators have begun to apologize for the texts rather than expound them. The objection misreads who is being indicted. In every case the unfaithful wife is the covenant people as a whole — priests, elders, kings, and congregation, overwhelmingly men — and the figure is chosen because marriage is the closest and most binding of human bonds and its betrayal the most wounding. God does not say Israel broke a rule. He says she broke a marriage. Soften the figure and you have softened the doctrine of the covenant, and with it the doctrine of grace, because the astonishing thing in Hosea is that the husband buys her back.

The subtler corruption is the assumption that idolatry requires an idol. Psalm 106:39 forecloses it: they went a whoring with their own inventions. Gideon’s ephod was made from the spoil of a victory God had given, by a man who had just refused the crown, and it became a snare to him and to his house. Calvin’s judgment that the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols is exactly this verse in a phrase. The question for a modern congregation is not whether it keeps a shrine but what it cannot be parted from, what it consults first, and what it would not surrender if God asked.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew zanah (H2181), to commit fornication, used figuratively of idolatry throughout; the noun zenunim (H2183), whoredoms, and taznuth (H8457) in Ezekiel.

expand to see more

Hebrew zanah (H2181) — to commit harlotry; the verb behind go a whoring after in every instance.

Hebrew zenunim (H2183) — whoredoms; Hosea 1:2, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms.

Hebrew na’aph (H5003) — to commit adultery; the companion figure, used of the covenant breach in Jeremiah 3:8.

Hebrew ephod (H646) — the priestly garment; Gideon’s became the object of Israel’s whoredom (Judges 8:27).

Greek porneia (G4202) — fornication; carried into Revelation 17 of the great harlot and her wine.

Usage

"They go a whoring after their gods (Exodus 34:15) — the warning issued before the land was entered."

"All Israel went thither a whoring after it (Judges 8:27) — a good man’s ephod becoming a snare."

"Went a whoring with their own inventions (Psalm 106:39) — idolatry needing no foreign shrine."
